When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). Dems Remain in Charge in California Governor and US House Races; Lead for Proposition 39 Narrows, But Support for Proposition 40 Drops:
Just over a week until votes are counted, SurveyUSA's latest statewide tracking poll for KGTV News 10 and the San Diego Union-Tribune shows no real change in 3 statewide contests, some
movement in another, and enough change in the 5th to potentially switch the outcome. Here's how it all breaks down:
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton each fall a nominal single point in the race for Governor from our last poll one month ago, leaving Becerra just where he was in September,
22 points ahead of Hilton, 54% to 32%, with 14% of voters undecided. Hilton last month led among four demographic groups, each of which continues to give him a double-digit advantage today:
by 75 points among conservatives, by 69 points among Republicans, by 65 points among 2024 Trump voters, and by 28 points among voters who say immigration is the biggest issue facing
California. This month, Hilton adds two new groups to his column: rural voters, where he leads by a nominal single point, a 6-point switch from one month ago, when Becerra had a 5-point
advantage ; and among a newly reported group, white evangelical voters, where Hilton leads by 41. Becerra leads meaningfully, by no fewer than 7 percentage points, throughout the rest of the
state and across all demographic subgroups.
The situation is virtually identical in generic US House balloting, where 58% of likely voters tell SurveyUSA they will vote for a Democratic candidate, unchanged from last month , and 32% say they
will vote for a Republican, down a nominal and statistically insignificant point. Generic Republicans run slightly ahead of Hilton among Republican voters (76-point margin for House, 69-point
margin for Governor) and Trump voters (73 points for House, 65 points for Governor); the numbers are roughly the same, within 2-3 points, among rural voters and conservatives; Hilton runs more
strongly than generic House candidates among white evangelicals (a 15-point difference, 41 points for Hilton vs. 26 points for Republican House candidates) and among voters most focused on
immigration (28 points vs. 14 points).
Any outcome is possible in the less-followed down-ballot race for the nonpartisan Superintendent of Public Instruction position. 41% of voters are undecided here, down from 53% in September .
34% of likely voters say they will vote for Richard Barrera, a Democrat and president of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education (up 8 points from 26% last month); 25% say they
will vote for Sonja Shaw, a Republican and president of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education (up 5 points from 20%). Last month, "undecided" was ahead of both candidates
with the only exceptions being voters under age 35 and those voters most focused on housing; today, undecided is the leading choice for fewer subgroups, but still leads in most. Notably, 21% of
those who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot say they don't recall how they voted in this contest – compared to 2% in the gubernatorial and 5% in the US House races.
Turning next to ballot measures, Proposition 39 , which would require voters to show government identification in order to vote, passes today by a sub-majority 7-point margin, 49% to 42%, with
10% of likely voters undecided. That's a 3-point net dip from last month , when 'yes' led 'no' by 10 points, 48% to 38%. Opposition to ballot measures typically rises as the election nears, and with 1
in 10 voters as yet undecided, any outcome is possible here. We note that among the 20% of the electorate who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot, the measure fails by a
13-point margin, while it leads by 9 points among those who say they are certain to vote this year and by 22 among those who say they probably will vote.
Proposition 40 , which would collect a one-time tax from billionaires, was up 8 points last month , 48% to 40%, but today leads by a single nominal point, 44% to 43%, with 13% undecided. Those
who have already voted say they voted no by a 35-point margin, 65% to 30%; those who say they are certain to vote support the measure by a 7-point margin, with 47% voting yes and 40% no;
among probable voters, it's a 21-point margin for yes, 49% to 28%. Given the shift from September to October here, Proposition 40 seems likely to fail.
Reviewing net approval ratings and looking at their month-on-month change, reporting them from highest to lowest: +5: Gavin Newsom. 48% today approve and 43% disapprove of the job
Newsom is doing as Governor; that's up from +2 in September. +0: The state legislature. 40% approve, 40% disapprove. That's up from -5 last month. -40: Donald Trump. 27% approve and 67%
disapprove. Last month, Trump was at -37 – a 3-point decline. -49: Congress. 17% approve, 66% disapprove; down one point from last month. Fully crosstabbed results, including additional

We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

Proposition 39
Require identification for voting
This initiative would require voters to show government-issued identification at the polls and order election officials to verify that all registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters who cast a mail-in ballot would need to give the last four digits of a government ID, such as a driver’s license number. California currently requires residents to provide an identification card and Social Security number to register to vote, but does not request it at polling places. It was placed on the ballot by conservative groups.

Summary
Support
Supporters argue that ID requirements at voting sites will strengthen voters’ trust in California’s election process, and that most states require voters to show some form of identification to vote.
Oppose
Opponents say requiring ID will make it harder for eligible voters who don’t have a driver’s license or other supporting documents to vote. They say this will disproportionately affect those with disabilities, who are low-income or have recently moved.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Voter ID measure falling short in new poll
By LINDSEY HOLDEN (https://www.politico.com/staff/lindsey-holden) and WILL MCCARTHY (https://www.politico.com/staff/will-mccarthy)
10/19/2026 04:16 PM EDT
Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio speaks at a press conference on July 16, 2025, in Sacramento, California, to announce a campaign to require voter identification in California. | Tran Nguyen/AP
PROBABLY NOT: California’s voter ID measure is falling short of majority support, with likely voters deeply divided along party lines, according to a new Citrin-POLITICO poll (https://www.politico.com/f/?id=000001a1-55a1-d4d9-adbd-f7ef88d30000).
Fifty-one percent of likely voters polled said they would vote against Proposition 39, which would require Californians to show ID at polling places and add the last few digits of an ID number to mail-in ballots. Forty-two percent said they would vote in favor of it, while 7% remained undecided.
Those results are in line with September polls from the Berkeley Institute for Governmental Studies (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3w14s99c) and the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/press-release/likely-voters-send-mixed-signals-on-billionaire-wealth-tax-becerra-maintains-wide-lead-over-hilton/), both of which had the measure losing by similar margins.
Voter ID has long been a priority of President Donald Trump . And while proponents of the California measure have sought to distance the campaign from the president, it remains highly polarizing.
Eighty percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said they would vote “no,” while 92% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents said they’re prepared to vote “yes."Independents favor the measure by a small margin, 45% to 41%.
“The independents, they’re very divided and they slightly lean to the yes side, but not by enough of a margin to make a difference, given the partisan division,” said Jack Citrin , a University of California, Berkeley, political science professor and co-director of the UC Berkeley Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research-POLITICO poll.
In the survey, 40% of registered voters said the measure, if passed, would make voting more secure, while 38% said it would make it harder for eligible voters to cast a ballot. Ten percent said it would have both effects, while 7% said neither.
Assessments were more critical in a concurrent survey of POLITICO’s audience of key political and policy influencers in the state — including political staffers, lobbyists, policy advisers and others deeply versed in California’s political landscape. Just 15% of those influentials said the measure would make elections more secure, while 69% said it would make it harder for eligible voters to cast a ballot.
Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio , who is leading the push for voter ID, has long cast the measure as bipartisan (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/04/californias-fight-against-voter-id-is-a-slow-burn-00905656), despite Democratic opposition. In an effort to court voters across the political spectrum, the campaign has run television ads (https://adm0.page.link/haks) featuring people talking about their Democratic and independent affiliations and bashing Trump.
By contrast, the No side has played into the partisan divide, calling Prop 39 a MAGA “power grab” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM) and tying it to Trump’s vocal opposition to mail-in voting.
Gavin Newsom , a co-chair of one of the No committees, says in a TV ad (https://adm0.page.link/eZe4) that Prop 39 “is a ploy by Trump’s billionaire allies to make it harder to vote and easier to throw out valid ballots.”
These data come from parallel surveys of California voters and policy influencers, fielded by TrueDot (https://www.truedot.ai/), the AI-accelerated research platform, in collaboration with the Citrin Center at UC Berkeley and POLITICO. Interviews for the voter survey were conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 9-14, among a sample of 1,149 registered voters, including 909 likely voters, selected at random through Verasight, with supplemental online panel recruitment. Voter results were weighted to California registered-voter benchmarks for age, educational attainment, race and ethnicity, gender, and geography, with additional calibration to the 2024 presidential vote by region.
From Oct. 14-16, a parallel study was conducted in partnership with POLITICO among its audience of key political and policy influencers in California. The audience was defined based on job title and organizational affiliation and included state and local government employees, political staffers, lobbyists, policy advisers, consultants, business decision-makers and subject matter experts.
The margin of error is plus or minus 3.2% for the registered voter sample and plus or minus 3.6% for likely voters. The influencer survey has no calculable error margin.

TOP OF THE TICKET
A highly subjective ranking of the ballot measures — past and future, certain and possible — getting our attention this week.
1. Props 41/42: Labor groups are organizing to defeat two countermeasures that would effectively void Prop 40, the wealth tax, should they pass. Groups associated with the California Federation of Teachers, California Labor Federation, United Domestic Workers and California School Employees Association all contributed six-figure checks to an opposition committee in the last two weeks.
2. Prop 38: Over the summer, the billionaire proponent of the immunology bond, Gary Michelson , expressed hope that California’s medical institutions would pony up to help pass his ballot measure. Two weeks before the election, the overwhelming majority of the campaign’s resources have come from Michelson alone.
3. Prop 45: Proponents of an effort to scale back elements of CEQA released a report last week showing that labor groups paid nearly $90 million (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/10/16/prop-45-unions-ceqa-law-firms-sacramento-bee/) to a pair of law firms that specialize in CEQA litigation. It’s part of an effort to convince voters that labor groups’ opposition to the measure is tied to their desire to weaponize the law for better working conditions, which labor groups denied. Opponents of Prop 45, meanwhile, are making the case that the measure would barely decrease monthly rents over the course of a decade.
4. Prop 43: Labor groups representing the state’s teachers and firefighters are contributing hundreds of thousands of dollars to the effort to defeat a measure that would raise the threshold for passing local taxes. Republican Assemblymember David Tangipa , meanwhile, spent part of last week campaigning for the tax measure in the Central Valley, arguing that Prop 43 would help small businesses, renters and homeowners.
5. Prop 40: The opposition campaign is warning of the words of professors who helped draft the wealth tax text, highlighting economist Emmanuel Saez ’s comments that the tax will “be an experiment.” The Yes on Prop 40 campaign faces a series of challenges in the lead up to the election, as our Jeremy B. White reported (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/15/california-wealth-tax-lagging-01119038) last week.
6. Prop 3: One of the committees organized to defeat Prop 39 is jumping into other ballot battles. The No on 39 Block Election Rigging committee, led in part by gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra , contributed $3 million from its coffers last week to help pass Prop 3, a measure to extend an existing tax on high earners.
7. Prop 44: The measure to regulate clinic spending seems to have been financially abandoned by its proponent, SEIU-UHW. The Yes committee has received no substantial contributions since May.
IN OTHER NEWS
TURNING RED: American voters across the political spectrum now assume most top tech CEOs are conservative, according to new results from The POLITICO Poll (https://www.politico.com/f/?id=000001a1-4fbf-dc9a-a9a3-5ffff0bb0000). And a plurality of voters say they believe tech is the biggest financial backer of the Republican Party, POLITICO’s Calder McHugh reports (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/poll-americans-big-tech-ceos-republican-01125853).
The results, first revealed in Decoded by POLITICO (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/decoded-by-politico), could complicate the prospects of Republicans trying to break from Trump in the midterms or 2028 amid rising backlash to Big Tech and AI. And they could spell trouble for the companies themselves next year if Democrats flip the House.
HELP WANTED: Lawmakers are under pressure to pass legislation to address the threats from advanced AI, but many have serious doubts they have the capacity to regulate the technology’s explosive growth, POLITICO’s Katherine Tully-McManus reports. (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/congress-ai-regulation-expertise-01123525)
Few are expecting lawmakers themselves — some of whom still proudly use flip phones — to become AI experts overnight. But while even congressional Luddites acknowledge there is urgency for Capitol Hill to quickly expand its expertise in tech policy to help with legislating, regulating and conducting effective oversight, there’s no consensus yet on how to achieve it.

About The Author : Lindsey Holden
Lindsey is a politics reporter based in Sacramento. She helms California Playbook PM, our must-read briefing on politics and government in the Golden State.
Before joining POLITICO, she reported on California politics and key state policy concerns around housing, crime and inequality for more than eight years at the Sacramento Bee and the San Luis Obispo Tribune.
A Southern California native raised in the Midwest, Lindsey attended DePaul University before pursuing a master’s degree at Northwestern's Medill School of Journalism.
About The Author : Will McCarthy
Will McCarthy is a California reporter at POLITICO with a focus on ballot measures and the state's ongoing experiment with direct democracy. Will co-helms a weekly newsletter and writes enterprise stories about the politics and policy surrounding California's lively initiative process as part of a first-of-its-kind ballot measure team.

Voter ID measure falling short in new poll
By LINDSEY HOLDEN (https://www.politico.com/staff/lindsey-holden) and WILL MCCARTHY (https://www.politico.com/staff/will-mccarthy)
10/19/2026 04:16 PM EDT
Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio speaks at a press conference on July 16, 2025, in Sacramento, California, to announce a campaign to require voter identification in California. | Tran Nguyen/AP
PROBABLY NOT: California’s voter ID measure is falling short of majority support, with likely voters deeply divided along party lines, according to a new Citrin-POLITICO poll (https://www.politico.com/f/?id=000001a1-55a1-d4d9-adbd-f7ef88d30000).
Fifty-one percent of likely voters polled said they would vote against Proposition 39, which would require Californians to show ID at polling places and add the last few digits of an ID number to mail-in ballots. Forty-two percent said they would vote in favor of it, while 7% remained undecided.
Those results are in line with September polls from the Berkeley Institute for Governmental Studies (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3w14s99c) and the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/press-release/likely-voters-send-mixed-signals-on-billionaire-wealth-tax-becerra-maintains-wide-lead-over-hilton/), both of which had the measure losing by similar margins.
Voter ID has long been a priority of President Donald Trump . And while proponents of the California measure have sought to distance the campaign from the president, it remains highly polarizing.
Eighty percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said they would vote “no,” while 92% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents said they’re prepared to vote “yes."Independents favor the measure by a small margin, 45% to 41%.
“The independents, they’re very divided and they slightly lean to the yes side, but not by enough of a margin to make a difference, given the partisan division,” said Jack Citrin , a University of California, Berkeley, political science professor and co-director of the UC Berkeley Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research-POLITICO poll.
In the survey, 40% of registered voters said the measure, if passed, would make voting more secure, while 38% said it would make it harder for eligible voters to cast a ballot. Ten percent said it would have both effects, while 7% said neither.
Assessments were more critical in a concurrent survey of POLITICO’s audience of key political and policy influencers in the state — including political staffers, lobbyists, policy advisers and others deeply versed in California’s political landscape. Just 15% of those influentials said the measure would make elections more secure, while 69% said it would make it harder for eligible voters to cast a ballot.
Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio , who is leading the push for voter ID, has long cast the measure as bipartisan (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/04/californias-fight-against-voter-id-is-a-slow-burn-00905656), despite Democratic opposition. In an effort to court voters across the political spectrum, the campaign has run television ads (https://adm0.page.link/haks) featuring people talking about their Democratic and independent affiliations and bashing Trump.
By contrast, the No side has played into the partisan divide, calling Prop 39 a MAGA “power grab” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM) and tying it to Trump’s vocal opposition to mail-in voting.
Gavin Newsom , a co-chair of one of the No committees, says in a TV ad (https://adm0.page.link/eZe4) that Prop 39 “is a ploy by Trump’s billionaire allies to make it harder to vote and easier to throw out valid ballots.”
These data come from parallel surveys of California voters and policy influencers, fielded by TrueDot (https://www.truedot.ai/), the AI-accelerated research platform, in collaboration with the Citrin Center at UC Berkeley and POLITICO. Interviews for the voter survey were conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 9-14, among a sample of 1,149 registered voters, including 909 likely voters, selected at random through Verasight, with supplemental online panel recruitment. Voter results were weighted to California registered-voter benchmarks for age, educational attainment, race and ethnicity, gender, and geography, with additional calibration to the 2024 presidential vote by region.
From Oct. 14-16, a parallel study was conducted in partnership with POLITICO among its audience of key political and policy influencers in California. The audience was defined based on job title and organizational affiliation and included state and local government employees, political staffers, lobbyists, policy advisers, consultants, business decision-makers and subject matter experts.
The margin of error is plus or minus 3.2% for the registered voter sample and plus or minus 3.6% for likely voters. The influencer survey has no calculable error margin.
Welcome to Ballot Measure Weekly , a special Monday edition of Playbook PM focused on California’s lively realm of ballot measure campaigns. Questions? Concerns? Tips? Drop ballot measures reporter Will McCarthy a line at [email protected] (https://www.politico.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#ddaab0bebebcafa9b5a49dadb2b1b4a9b4beb2f3beb2b0) .
TOP OF THE TICKET
A highly subjective ranking of the ballot measures — past and future, certain and possible — getting our attention this week.
1. Props 41/42: Labor groups are organizing to defeat two countermeasures that would effectively void Prop 40, the wealth tax, should they pass. Groups associated with the California Federation of Teachers, California Labor Federation, United Domestic Workers and California School Employees Association all contributed six-figure checks to an opposition committee in the last two weeks.
2. Prop 38: Over the summer, the billionaire proponent of the immunology bond, Gary Michelson , expressed hope that California’s medical institutions would pony up to help pass his ballot measure. Two weeks before the election, the overwhelming majority of the campaign’s resources have come from Michelson alone.
3. Prop 45: Proponents of an effort to scale back elements of CEQA released a report last week showing that labor groups paid nearly $90 million (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/10/16/prop-45-unions-ceqa-law-firms-sacramento-bee/) to a pair of law firms that specialize in CEQA litigation. It’s part of an effort to convince voters that labor groups’ opposition to the measure is tied to their desire to weaponize the law for better working conditions, which labor groups denied. Opponents of Prop 45, meanwhile, are making the case that the measure would barely decrease monthly rents over the course of a decade.
4. Prop 43: Labor groups representing the state’s teachers and firefighters are contributing hundreds of thousands of dollars to the effort to defeat a measure that would raise the threshold for passing local taxes. Republican Assemblymember David Tangipa , meanwhile, spent part of last week campaigning for the tax measure in the Central Valley, arguing that Prop 43 would help small businesses, renters and homeowners.
5. Prop 40: The opposition campaign is warning of the words of professors who helped draft the wealth tax text, highlighting economist Emmanuel Saez ’s comments that the tax will “be an experiment.” The Yes on Prop 40 campaign faces a series of challenges in the lead up to the election, as our Jeremy B. White reported (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/15/california-wealth-tax-lagging-01119038) last week.
6. Prop 3: One of the committees organized to defeat Prop 39 is jumping into other ballot battles. The No on 39 Block Election Rigging committee, led in part by gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra , contributed $3 million from its coffers last week to help pass Prop 3, a measure to extend an existing tax on high earners.
7. Prop 44: The measure to regulate clinic spending seems to have been financially abandoned by its proponent, SEIU-UHW. The Yes committee has received no substantial contributions since May.
IN OTHER NEWS
TURNING RED: American voters across the political spectrum now assume most top tech CEOs are conservative, according to new results from The POLITICO Poll (https://www.politico.com/f/?id=000001a1-4fbf-dc9a-a9a3-5ffff0bb0000). And a plurality of voters say they believe tech is the biggest financial backer of the Republican Party, POLITICO’s Calder McHugh reports (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/poll-americans-big-tech-ceos-republican-01125853).
The results, first revealed in Decoded by POLITICO (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/decoded-by-politico), could complicate the prospects of Republicans trying to break from Trump in the midterms or 2028 amid rising backlash to Big Tech and AI. And they could spell trouble for the companies themselves next year if Democrats flip the House.
HELP WANTED: Lawmakers are under pressure to pass legislation to address the threats from advanced AI, but many have serious doubts they have the capacity to regulate the technology’s explosive growth, POLITICO’s Katherine Tully-McManus reports. (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/congress-ai-regulation-expertise-01123525)
Few are expecting lawmakers themselves — some of whom still proudly use flip phones — to become AI experts overnight. But while even congressional Luddites acknowledge there is urgency for Capitol Hill to quickly expand its expertise in tech policy to help with legislating, regulating and conducting effective oversight, there’s no consensus yet on how to achieve it.

Voter ID measure falling short in new poll
By LINDSEY HOLDEN (https://www.politico.com/staff/lindsey-holden) and WILL MCCARTHY (https://www.politico.com/staff/will-mccarthy)
10/19/2026 04:16 PM EDT
Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio speaks at a press conference on July 16, 2025, in Sacramento, California, to announce a campaign to require voter identification in California. | Tran Nguyen/AP
PROBABLY NOT: California’s voter ID measure is falling short of majority support, with likely voters deeply divided along party lines, according to a new Citrin-POLITICO poll (https://www.politico.com/f/?id=000001a1-55a1-d4d9-adbd-f7ef88d30000).
Fifty-one percent of likely voters polled said they would vote against Proposition 39, which would require Californians to show ID at polling places and add the last few digits of an ID number to mail-in ballots. Forty-two percent said they would vote in favor of it, while 7% remained undecided.
Those results are in line with September polls from the Berkeley Institute for Governmental Studies (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3w14s99c) and the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/press-release/likely-voters-send-mixed-signals-on-billionaire-wealth-tax-becerra-maintains-wide-lead-over-hilton/), both of which had the measure losing by similar margins.
Voter ID has long been a priority of President Donald Trump . And while proponents of the California measure have sought to distance the campaign from the president, it remains highly polarizing.
Eighty percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said they would vote “no,” while 92% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents said they’re prepared to vote “yes."Independents favor the measure by a small margin, 45% to 41%.
“The independents, they’re very divided and they slightly lean to the yes side, but not by enough of a margin to make a difference, given the partisan division,” said Jack Citrin , a University of California, Berkeley, political science professor and co-director of the UC Berkeley Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research-POLITICO poll.
In the survey, 40% of registered voters said the measure, if passed, would make voting more secure, while 38% said it would make it harder for eligible voters to cast a ballot. Ten percent said it would have both effects, while 7% said neither.
Assessments were more critical in a concurrent survey of POLITICO’s audience of key political and policy influencers in the state — including political staffers, lobbyists, policy advisers and others deeply versed in California’s political landscape. Just 15% of those influentials said the measure would make elections more secure, while 69% said it would make it harder for eligible voters to cast a ballot.
Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio , who is leading the push for voter ID, has long cast the measure as bipartisan (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/04/californias-fight-against-voter-id-is-a-slow-burn-00905656), despite Democratic opposition. In an effort to court voters across the political spectrum, the campaign has run television ads (https://adm0.page.link/haks) featuring people talking about their Democratic and independent affiliations and bashing Trump.
By contrast, the No side has played into the partisan divide, calling Prop 39 a MAGA “power grab” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM) and tying it to Trump’s vocal opposition to mail-in voting.
Gavin Newsom , a co-chair of one of the No committees, says in a TV ad (https://adm0.page.link/eZe4) that Prop 39 “is a ploy by Trump’s billionaire allies to make it harder to vote and easier to throw out valid ballots.”
These data come from parallel surveys of California voters and policy influencers, fielded by TrueDot (https://www.truedot.ai/), the AI-accelerated research platform, in collaboration with the Citrin Center at UC Berkeley and POLITICO. Interviews for the voter survey were conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 9-14, among a sample of 1,149 registered voters, including 909 likely voters, selected at random through Verasight, with supplemental online panel recruitment. Voter results were weighted to California registered-voter benchmarks for age, educational attainment, race and ethnicity, gender, and geography, with additional calibration to the 2024 presidential vote by region.
From Oct. 14-16, a parallel study was conducted in partnership with POLITICO among its audience of key political and policy influencers in California. The audience was defined based on job title and organizational affiliation and included state and local government employees, political staffers, lobbyists, policy advisers, consultants, business decision-makers and subject matter experts.
The margin of error is plus or minus 3.2% for the registered voter sample and plus or minus 3.6% for likely voters. The influencer survey has no calculable error margin.

TOP OF THE TICKET
A highly subjective ranking of the ballot measures — past and future, certain and possible — getting our attention this week.
1. Props 41/42: Labor groups are organizing to defeat two countermeasures that would effectively void Prop 40, the wealth tax, should they pass. Groups associated with the California Federation of Teachers, California Labor Federation, United Domestic Workers and California School Employees Association all contributed six-figure checks to an opposition committee in the last two weeks.
2. Prop 38: Over the summer, the billionaire proponent of the immunology bond, Gary Michelson , expressed hope that California’s medical institutions would pony up to help pass his ballot measure. Two weeks before the election, the overwhelming majority of the campaign’s resources have come from Michelson alone.
3. Prop 45: Proponents of an effort to scale back elements of CEQA released a report last week showing that labor groups paid nearly $90 million (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/10/16/prop-45-unions-ceqa-law-firms-sacramento-bee/) to a pair of law firms that specialize in CEQA litigation. It’s part of an effort to convince voters that labor groups’ opposition to the measure is tied to their desire to weaponize the law for better working conditions, which labor groups denied. Opponents of Prop 45, meanwhile, are making the case that the measure would barely decrease monthly rents over the course of a decade.
4. Prop 43: Labor groups representing the state’s teachers and firefighters are contributing hundreds of thousands of dollars to the effort to defeat a measure that would raise the threshold for passing local taxes. Republican Assemblymember David Tangipa , meanwhile, spent part of last week campaigning for the tax measure in the Central Valley, arguing that Prop 43 would help small businesses, renters and homeowners.
5. Prop 40: The opposition campaign is warning of the words of professors who helped draft the wealth tax text, highlighting economist Emmanuel Saez ’s comments that the tax will “be an experiment.” The Yes on Prop 40 campaign faces a series of challenges in the lead up to the election, as our Jeremy B. White reported (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/15/california-wealth-tax-lagging-01119038) last week.
6. Prop 3: One of the committees organized to defeat Prop 39 is jumping into other ballot battles. The No on 39 Block Election Rigging committee, led in part by gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra , contributed $3 million from its coffers last week to help pass Prop 3, a measure to extend an existing tax on high earners.
7. Prop 44: The measure to regulate clinic spending seems to have been financially abandoned by its proponent, SEIU-UHW. The Yes committee has received no substantial contributions since May.
IN OTHER NEWS
TURNING RED: American voters across the political spectrum now assume most top tech CEOs are conservative, according to new results from The POLITICO Poll (https://www.politico.com/f/?id=000001a1-4fbf-dc9a-a9a3-5ffff0bb0000). And a plurality of voters say they believe tech is the biggest financial backer of the Republican Party, POLITICO’s Calder McHugh reports (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/poll-americans-big-tech-ceos-republican-01125853).
The results, first revealed in Decoded by POLITICO (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/decoded-by-politico), could complicate the prospects of Republicans trying to break from Trump in the midterms or 2028 amid rising backlash to Big Tech and AI. And they could spell trouble for the companies themselves next year if Democrats flip the House.
HELP WANTED: Lawmakers are under pressure to pass legislation to address the threats from advanced AI, but many have serious doubts they have the capacity to regulate the technology’s explosive growth, POLITICO’s Katherine Tully-McManus reports. (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/congress-ai-regulation-expertise-01123525)
Few are expecting lawmakers themselves — some of whom still proudly use flip phones — to become AI experts overnight. But while even congressional Luddites acknowledge there is urgency for Capitol Hill to quickly expand its expertise in tech policy to help with legislating, regulating and conducting effective oversight, there’s no consensus yet on how to achieve it.

About The Author : Lindsey Holden
Lindsey is a politics reporter based in Sacramento. She helms California Playbook PM, our must-read briefing on politics and government in the Golden State.
Before joining POLITICO, she reported on California politics and key state policy concerns around housing, crime and inequality for more than eight years at the Sacramento Bee and the San Luis Obispo Tribune.
A Southern California native raised in the Midwest, Lindsey attended DePaul University before pursuing a master’s degree at Northwestern's Medill School of Journalism.
About The Author : Will McCarthy
Will McCarthy is a California reporter at POLITICO with a focus on ballot measures and the state's ongoing experiment with direct democracy. Will co-helms a weekly newsletter and writes enterprise stories about the politics and policy surrounding California's lively initiative process as part of a first-of-its-kind ballot measure team.
He's covered environmental justice group's efforts to hold big industries accountable through the initiative process (https://www.politico.com/news/2024/09/03/richmond-california-chevron-oil-00176922), the powerful impact ballot measures can have on legislative negotiations, and their role in the national debate over soda taxes. He also specializes in local measures, and how citizen-driven ballot measure efforts reflect the color and characters of cities and towns across the state.
Previously, Will covered Alameda County government for the San Jose Mercury News and city politics at an NPR affiliate in rural Alaska. He holds a masters degree in journalism from UC Berkeley.

Voter ID measure falling short in new poll
By LINDSEY HOLDEN (https://www.politico.com/staff/lindsey-holden) and WILL MCCARTHY (https://www.politico.com/staff/will-mccarthy)
10/19/2026 04:16 PM EDT
Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio speaks at a press conference on July 16, 2025, in Sacramento, California, to announce a campaign to require voter identification in California. | Tran Nguyen/AP
PROBABLY NOT: California’s voter ID measure is falling short of majority support, with likely voters deeply divided along party lines, according to a new Citrin-POLITICO poll (https://www.politico.com/f/?id=000001a1-55a1-d4d9-adbd-f7ef88d30000).
Fifty-one percent of likely voters polled said they would vote against Proposition 39, which would require Californians to show ID at polling places and add the last few digits of an ID number to mail-in ballots. Forty-two percent said they would vote in favor of it, while 7% remained undecided.
Those results are in line with September polls from the Berkeley Institute for Governmental Studies (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3w14s99c) and the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/press-release/likely-voters-send-mixed-signals-on-billionaire-wealth-tax-becerra-maintains-wide-lead-over-hilton/), both of which had the measure losing by similar margins.
Voter ID has long been a priority of President Donald Trump . And while proponents of the California measure have sought to distance the campaign from the president, it remains highly polarizing.
Eighty percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents said they would vote “no,” while 92% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents said they’re prepared to vote “yes."Independents favor the measure by a small margin, 45% to 41%.
“The independents, they’re very divided and they slightly lean to the yes side, but not by enough of a margin to make a difference, given the partisan division,” said Jack Citrin , a University of California, Berkeley, political science professor and co-director of the UC Berkeley Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research-POLITICO poll.
In the survey, 40% of registered voters said the measure, if passed, would make voting more secure, while 38% said it would make it harder for eligible voters to cast a ballot. Ten percent said it would have both effects, while 7% said neither.
Assessments were more critical in a concurrent survey of POLITICO’s audience of key political and policy influencers in the state — including political staffers, lobbyists, policy advisers and others deeply versed in California’s political landscape. Just 15% of those influentials said the measure would make elections more secure, while 69% said it would make it harder for eligible voters to cast a ballot.
Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio , who is leading the push for voter ID, has long cast the measure as bipartisan (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/04/californias-fight-against-voter-id-is-a-slow-burn-00905656), despite Democratic opposition. In an effort to court voters across the political spectrum, the campaign has run television ads (https://adm0.page.link/haks) featuring people talking about their Democratic and independent affiliations and bashing Trump.
By contrast, the No side has played into the partisan divide, calling Prop 39 a MAGA “power grab” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM) and tying it to Trump’s vocal opposition to mail-in voting.
Gavin Newsom , a co-chair of one of the No committees, says in a TV ad (https://adm0.page.link/eZe4) that Prop 39 “is a ploy by Trump’s billionaire allies to make it harder to vote and easier to throw out valid ballots.”
These data come from parallel surveys of California voters and policy influencers, fielded by TrueDot (https://www.truedot.ai/), the AI-accelerated research platform, in collaboration with the Citrin Center at UC Berkeley and POLITICO. Interviews for the voter survey were conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 9-14, among a sample of 1,149 registered voters, including 909 likely voters, selected at random through Verasight, with supplemental online panel recruitment. Voter results were weighted to California registered-voter benchmarks for age, educational attainment, race and ethnicity, gender, and geography, with additional calibration to the 2024 presidential vote by region.
From Oct. 14-16, a parallel study was conducted in partnership with POLITICO among its audience of key political and policy influencers in California. The audience was defined based on job title and organizational affiliation and included state and local government employees, political staffers, lobbyists, policy advisers, consultants, business decision-makers and subject matter experts.
The margin of error is plus or minus 3.2% for the registered voter sample and plus or minus 3.6% for likely voters. The influencer survey has no calculable error margin.

TOP OF THE TICKET
A highly subjective ranking of the ballot measures — past and future, certain and possible — getting our attention this week.
1. Props 41/42: Labor groups are organizing to defeat two countermeasures that would effectively void Prop 40, the wealth tax, should they pass. Groups associated with the California Federation of Teachers, California Labor Federation, United Domestic Workers and California School Employees Association all contributed six-figure checks to an opposition committee in the last two weeks.
2. Prop 38: Over the summer, the billionaire proponent of the immunology bond, Gary Michelson , expressed hope that California’s medical institutions would pony up to help pass his ballot measure. Two weeks before the election, the overwhelming majority of the campaign’s resources have come from Michelson alone.
3. Prop 45: Proponents of an effort to scale back elements of CEQA released a report last week showing that labor groups paid nearly $90 million (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/10/16/prop-45-unions-ceqa-law-firms-sacramento-bee/) to a pair of law firms that specialize in CEQA litigation. It’s part of an effort to convince voters that labor groups’ opposition to the measure is tied to their desire to weaponize the law for better working conditions, which labor groups denied. Opponents of Prop 45, meanwhile, are making the case that the measure would barely decrease monthly rents over the course of a decade.
4. Prop 43: Labor groups representing the state’s teachers and firefighters are contributing hundreds of thousands of dollars to the effort to defeat a measure that would raise the threshold for passing local taxes. Republican Assemblymember David Tangipa , meanwhile, spent part of last week campaigning for the tax measure in the Central Valley, arguing that Prop 43 would help small businesses, renters and homeowners.
5. Prop 40: The opposition campaign is warning of the words of professors who helped draft the wealth tax text, highlighting economist Emmanuel Saez ’s comments that the tax will “be an experiment.” The Yes on Prop 40 campaign faces a series of challenges in the lead up to the election, as our Jeremy B. White reported (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/15/california-wealth-tax-lagging-01119038) last week.
6. Prop 3: One of the committees organized to defeat Prop 39 is jumping into other ballot battles. The No on 39 Block Election Rigging committee, led in part by gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra , contributed $3 million from its coffers last week to help pass Prop 3, a measure to extend an existing tax on high earners.
7. Prop 44: The measure to regulate clinic spending seems to have been financially abandoned by its proponent, SEIU-UHW. The Yes committee has received no substantial contributions since May.
IN OTHER NEWS
TURNING RED: American voters across the political spectrum now assume most top tech CEOs are conservative, according to new results from The POLITICO Poll (https://www.politico.com/f/?id=000001a1-4fbf-dc9a-a9a3-5ffff0bb0000). And a plurality of voters say they believe tech is the biggest financial backer of the Republican Party, POLITICO’s Calder McHugh reports (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/poll-americans-big-tech-ceos-republican-01125853).
The results, first revealed in Decoded by POLITICO (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/decoded-by-politico), could complicate the prospects of Republicans trying to break from Trump in the midterms or 2028 amid rising backlash to Big Tech and AI. And they could spell trouble for the companies themselves next year if Democrats flip the House.
HELP WANTED: Lawmakers are under pressure to pass legislation to address the threats from advanced AI, but many have serious doubts they have the capacity to regulate the technology’s explosive growth, POLITICO’s Katherine Tully-McManus reports. (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/congress-ai-regulation-expertise-01123525)
Few are expecting lawmakers themselves — some of whom still proudly use flip phones — to become AI experts overnight. But while even congressional Luddites acknowledge there is urgency for Capitol Hill to quickly expand its expertise in tech policy to help with legislating, regulating and conducting effective oversight, there’s no consensus yet on how to achieve it.

Is California’s Proposed Billionaire Tax in Trouble? New Polls Find Bad News
Two public nonpartisan surveys show Proposition 40 trailing in the final days of voting. Meanwhile, an initiative to require voter ID in California is losing by double digits.
Oct 29, 2026
Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) speaks at a rally dubbed "Ballots Over Billionaires" at The Novo on Oct. 5, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders joined Khanna for the event in support of Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of approximately 200 California billionaires, with most of the revenue intended to offset cuts to Medi-Cal and other healthcare services. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
A proposal to tax California’s billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12106033/the-political-calculus-behind-newsoms-opposition-to-californias-billionaire-tax) to fund healthcare is trailing in two public, nonpartisan polls released this week, surveys that also found strong opposition to a separate ballot measure that would require voters to show identification at the polls.
Proposition 40 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40), which would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the overall wealth of the state’s billionaires, was tracking below the majority needed to pass in polls from both UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California. With days left to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm election, IGS found just 8% of likely voters still undecided on the measure, which billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12104645/sf-billionaire-chris-larsen-on-ai-this-is-an-incredibly-dangerous-moment) have spent more than $300 million to defeat.
Proposition 39 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-39), the voter ID initiative, was also trailing by 20 points in the IGS poll, with just 37% of likely voters saying they were voting yes and 5% undecided. PPIC’s poll found slightly stronger support for the measure, but still had it losing.
Support for Proposition 40 appears to be slipping heading into Election Day. Last month’s PPIC poll had a slim majority in favor before the slide this month.
But in the IGS poll released this week, half of likely voters said they will vote no on Proposition 40, while 42% said they are voting yes. That’s a shift from last month, when the IGS poll found 42% of voters against the measure and 45% backing it.
A T-shirt with a campaign message is seen before the start of a rally led by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, during the campaign kickoff for the California Billionaire Tax Act at The Wiltern in Los Angeles, on Feb. 18, 2026. Sanders is seeking the support of California voters for a November ballot initiative of an emergency tax on billionaires to help the state’s healthcare system. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
Mark DiCamillo, director of the IGS Poll, said the No on Proposition 40 side is clearly benefiting from the huge amounts of money being poured into defeating the wealth tax.
“A well-funded no side campaign usually has the advantage over yes campaigns, just because all they have to do is raise doubts,” he said.
The poll found Proposition 40 backed by strong majorities of Democrats and voters under 40, and opposed by Republicans and voters over 50. Independents are split.
DiCamillo said the disparity between how younger and older voters view the proposed tax is indicative of a growing split that did not used to exist among the California electorate.
From the 2026 Voter Guide
Learn about Proposition 40 and its supporters, opponents, and arguments (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40)
“The generational divide is growing over time, just because the younger set is having a hard time. They can’t afford a house, they can’t reach the American dream,” he said.
“Those are the segments that are now migrating to the Democratic socialists…. They really don’t like the disparity in wealth.”
The fate of the proposed wealth tax will not swing solely on Proposition 40.
Both polls also showed close contests in Propositions 41 and 42, measures put on the ballot by billionaires with language that would nullify the tax if they pass with more votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 41 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-41) would require ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by “special” taxes — those earmarked for a specific purpose. It also would make any new special taxes subject to the state’s existing spending limit. Proposition 42 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-42) would prohibit new taxes on financial assets — such as stocks — and other personal property, and also prohibit most retroactive taxes.
While IGS’s survey showed Propositions 41 and 42 slightly ahead, DiCamillo noted they also found double-digit percentages of likely voters still undecided — and those who have moved since IGS’s September survey have largely turned against the billionaire-backed measures.
“The no side has gained 11 [points] while the yes side is static,” DiCamillo said of Proposition 42.
Proposition 39, the voter ID measure placed on the ballot by Republican lawmakers, has also lost ground since IGS’s poll last month, with the no side gaining 7 percentage points. The survey found Republicans are the only group backing the measure. Likely voters who list no party preference are against it by a 15-point margin in the IGS poll, and majorities of voters in nearly all subgroups — age, race and gender — are opposed.
Sen. Tony Strickland speaks at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on Monday, March 2, 2026, for a press conference highlighting voter signatures in favor of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot. (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)
PPIC found similar opposition: That survey has Proposition 39 down by 17 points, with 58% of likely voters saying they will vote no.
DiCamillo said voters appear to be linking the voter ID measure to President Donald Trump’s push for changes to election laws, which are unpopular with Democrats and independents.
“I think Trump is a factor,” he said. “That really is the winning argument: You go after Trump.”
PPIC also polled on Proposition 45 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-45), the ballot measure written by the California Chamber of Commerce to speed up environmental reviews of construction projects. The survey found likely voters split on the changes to the California Environmental Quality Act, with 46% saying they are voting yes and 50% voting no.
The IGS poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 19-25, and included 2,787 registered voters. The PPIC poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 16-22 and included 1,728 California adult residents.
Both polls have a sampling error of plus or minus 3%.
